account:
It is day 1, shortly after nine, and I am in the town hall office preparing for my ten o'clock grain inspection at the mill. I have read today's appointment book and returned it to the secretary. My later appointments are lunch at home, council letters at one, private tea at the neighbour's cottage at three, office at half past four, and home at seven.

The unusual thing is that both the secretary and baker have been unable to find the miller at the mill. The secretary checked last evening and this morning; the baker also checked this morning. I do not know why the miller is absent, and this alone does not establish a problem. Freight and the neighbour are supposed to relay my request for grain stock and delivery records for the inspection. That request is routine fact-finding, not authorization to spend.

The builder asked for repair work, but neither he nor I has a confirmed damage report. He agreed not to incur costs or begin work without agreement. There is no confirmed bridge or port change to announce. The secretary reports no new council correspondence or office requests, and the office chest has contained the filed accounts records. Those records distinguish my reported treasury balance from verified income and expenses.

The neighbour has been exchanging greetings and news with me and the baker, and has confirmed our tea. The baker has been asking whether any gatherings require bread; neither the secretary nor I knows of a confirmed public order. The secretary explicitly clarified that my tea is private, not town catering. This seems to be ordinary efforts to find business and prepare for the day, rather than evidence of any organized public event. Some nearby speech was indistinct, so I cannot infer its contents. My next priority is to reach the mill for the scheduled inspection and learn what can actually be established there.
